why_how.text: Rules and car basics are not enough, so safe driving also depends on judgment, patience and common sense.
Skill grows with supervised practice and can fade when experienced drivers stop paying attention.
Aggressive driving is common and deadly, and answering it in kind can turn into road rage.

scenario.text: Rob, an experienced driver, notices he arrived home with no memory of the drive.

reasoning.text: Experienced middle-aged drivers can become complacent, and driving on autopilot leaves them less tuned to the risks around them.

result.text: Rob resolves to stay alert and scan actively on familiar routes.

claim.text: Myth: experienced drivers no longer need to pay close attention.

correction.text: Experienced drivers can become complacent, and driving on autopilot leaves them less tuned to the risks around them.

prompt.text: A driver tailgates, weaves between lanes and flashes headlights at others. What kind of driving is this?

rationale.text: Aggressive drivers speed, tailgate, weave, pass illegally on the right, and may gesture, yell, honk or flash headlights.

narration.text: This lesson is about the driver, not the car. Safe driving takes more than vehicle basics and memorized rules. It also needs good judgment, reflexes, experience, patience and common sense. We will look at how teens build skill, why experienced drivers can slip into autopilot, how older drivers can sharpen their skills, and what aggressive driving looks like. Aggressive driving is one of the most serious risks on the road, so we will also look at how it can escalate. These ideas are less about one rule and more about the attitude you bring to every trip, whatever your age or experience.

A teen's skill and confidence grow through practice. First comes the driver education range. Then practice with a parent, guardian or designated licensed adult twenty-one or older. Later, once licensed, the teen drives alone. Each stage adds experience in a safer setting before the next step. This matters because judgment, reflexes and patience are not learned from a book. They are built behind the wheel, mile by mile. So the supervised stages are not a formality. They are where a new driver learns to read traffic, plan ahead and react calmly before facing the road with no one in the passenger seat.

Experienced middle-aged drivers can become complacent. Driving on autopilot leaves them less tuned to the risks around them. A familiar route can feel so routine that the driver stops scanning for hazards. Older drivers can improve through added training. AAA RoadWise Driver and AARP Driver Safety offer refresher courses, listed at Michigan.gov slash AgingDriver. So no driver is ever finished learning. New drivers build skill, experienced drivers must guard against autopilot, and older drivers can keep skills sharp with a refresher. At every age, active attention is what keeps experience working for you instead of against you.

Aggressive drivers run stop signs and red lights, speed, tailgate, weave, pass illegally on the right, and may gesture, yell, honk or flash their headlights. Federal highway safety officials have estimated that aggressive driving behaviors cause sixty-six percent of all traffic fatalities. That makes aggression one of the biggest threats on the road. Answering aggression in kind can escalate into road rage, where a weapon or the vehicle itself is used to attack another driver. So when you meet an aggressive driver, the safest choice is never to compete. Let them go, and keep your own driving calm.

lines.text: Trap: show them they were wrong.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When another driver acts aggressively, it is tempting to answer back with a honk, a gesture or a burst of speed. That is wrong. Answering aggression in kind can escalate into road rage, where a weapon or the vehicle itself is used to attack another driver. Options may suggest teaching the other driver a lesson, or blocking them to prove a point. Both are wrong. The goal is not to win an argument on the road. It is to get home safely. Patience and distance protect you far better than any response you could give in the moment.

Here is a quick check: a driver ahead tailgates other cars, weaves between lanes, and flashes headlights at people in the way. What kind of driving is this? Recall the list of aggressive behaviors. Aggressive drivers run stop signs and red lights, speed, tailgate, weave, pass illegally on the right, and may gesture, yell, honk or flash their headlights. So the answer is aggressive driving. The right response is to stay out of that driver's way. The next lesson covers exactly how to handle an aggressive driver without escalating the situation.

To finish, safe driving takes more than vehicle basics and rules. It needs good judgment, reflexes, experience, patience and common sense. Teens build skill on the driver education range, then with a parent, guardian or licensed adult twenty-one or older, and later alone. Experienced drivers can become complacent on autopilot, and older drivers can improve through refresher courses. Aggressive drivers speed, tailgate, weave and pass illegally, officials have estimated aggressive driving causes sixty-six percent of traffic fatalities, and answering in kind can escalate into road rage. The hook is patience beats aggression.

why_how.text: Giving room and letting others pass removes the conflict before it grows.
Avoiding gestures and eye contact keeps a confrontation from escalating.
Reporting aggressive drivers and crashes to police helps keep others safe.

scenario.text: A driver tailgates Kim on a two-lane road, staying inches from her bumper.

reasoning.text: If another driver tailgates you, pull over and let them pass, so the unsafe driver is ahead where you can see them.

result.text: Kim pulls over at a safe spot and lets the tailgater go by.

claim.text: Common mistake: slowing down or braking to teach a tailgater a lesson.

correction.text: If another driver tailgates you, pull over and let them pass, so they are ahead where you can see them.

prompt.text: An aggressive driver pulls beside you, yelling and gesturing. What should you do?

answer.text: Get out of the way, avoid eye contact, ignore the gestures, and report them when safe.

rationale.text: When confronted by an aggressive driver, get out of the way, avoid eye contact, ignore gestures or insults, and call police when safe.

narration.text: This lesson covers how to respond when other drivers behave badly. You cannot control another driver, but you can control your response, and the right response keeps a bad situation from getting worse. We will look at merging courteously, handling a tailgater while you pass and while you drive, dealing with gestures, getting away from a confrontation, and what to do if an aggressive driver crashes ahead. The common thread is distance. Every rule in this lesson puts more space between you and the aggressive driver, and none of them asks you to prove anything.

lines.text: Bad merge? Slow down, give room.

narration.text: Merge smoothly yourself. When another driver merges or turns badly, slow down, give room, and back off rather than trying to prove a point. If someone tailgates you while you pass in the left lane, move back right when safe and let faster traffic go. A backed-up left lane tempts aggressive drivers to take risks. If another driver tailgates you at other times, pull over and let them pass. That puts the unsafe driver ahead of you, where you can see them, instead of behind you, where they could hit you if you had to stop. Either way, the answer is to let them go.

lines.text: Confronted? Get away, avoid eye contact.

narration.text: Never gesture at other drivers in anger. If you made a mistake and someone gestures at you, signal that you are sorry. A simple apology often ends the moment. When confronted by an aggressive driver, get out of the way, avoid eye contact, and ignore gestures or insults. Call police to report the driver when it is safe to do so. Eye contact can feel like a challenge to an angry driver, so looking away is a way of stepping back. Your aim is to become uninteresting to the aggressive driver, so they move on and leave you alone.

If an aggressive driver crashes farther ahead, stop a safe distance from the scene, wait for police, and report what you saw. Your report can help police understand what happened. But stopping too close can put you in danger, from traffic or from the driver who caused the crash. So choose a safe place well back from the scene. Do not confront the driver. Let the police handle it, and give them a clear account of the driving you observed. Being a calm witness is one more way a patient driver helps keep the road safe for everyone.

lines.text: Trap: brake to teach a tailgater.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When someone tailgates, some drivers tap their brakes or slow down to teach the tailgater a lesson. That is wrong. If another driver tailgates you, pull over and let them pass, so the unsafe driver is ahead where you can see them. If it happens while you are passing in the left lane, move back right when safe and let faster traffic go. Options may suggest speeding up to get away, or holding your position to make a point. Both are wrong. Each of those keeps the aggressive driver close. Letting them go puts the danger in front of you, in view.

Here is a quick check: an aggressive driver pulls beside you, yelling and gesturing. What should you do? Recall the rule for confrontations. When confronted by an aggressive driver, get out of the way, avoid eye contact, ignore gestures or insults, and call police to report them when safe. So the answer is to move away from the driver without looking at them or reacting, and to report them once it is safe to make the call. Never gesture back. If you made a mistake that started it, a simple signal that you are sorry can calm things down.

To finish, merge smoothly, and when another driver merges or turns badly, slow down, give room and back off. If someone tailgates you while you pass in the left lane, move back right when safe. If another driver tailgates you, pull over and let them pass so they are ahead where you can see them. Never gesture in anger, and if you made a mistake, signal that you are sorry. When confronted, get out of the way, avoid eye contact, ignore insults and report the driver when safe. If an aggressive driver crashes ahead, stop a safe distance away and report what you saw. The hook is let tailgaters go ahead.

why_how.text: Intersection crashes cause more deaths and serious injuries than crashes anywhere else on the road.
Many things meet at an intersection, so you check them all and let others go first when unsure.
A blocked view hides cross traffic, so you creep forward until you can see.

scenario.text: At a corner, a parked truck blocks Ivy's view of cross traffic.

reasoning.text: When trees, buildings or snow piles block your view at an intersection, creep forward slowly until you can see past them.

result.text: Ivy edges forward until she can see both ways, then goes when clear.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming the other driver will do what you expect at an intersection.

correction.text: Let others go first whenever you are unsure what they will do.

prompt.text: At an intersection, you glance and see no cars, but a motorcycle could be hidden. What should you do?

answer.text: Look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

rationale.text: Their speed and distance are hard to judge, so look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds at intersections.

lines.text: The deadliest part of the road.

narration.text: This lesson is about intersections. Intersection crashes cause more traffic deaths and serious injuries than crashes on any other part of the road. That is because so many paths cross in one place: cars going straight and turning, pedestrians, bicyclists, motorcycles, and drivers watching signals and signs. We will look at what to check as you approach an intersection, why to look twice for smaller road users, and what to do when your view is blocked. Practice questions often ask what to do when you are unsure of another driver, so we will be clear about that rule and the reason behind it.

Approaching an intersection, check oncoming and cross traffic, pedestrians, signals, signs, markings, road condition and blind areas. Let others go first whenever you are unsure what they will do. That last rule is important. You cannot read every driver's mind, and assuming another driver will yield is how many intersection crashes begin. If a driver is hesitating, or you cannot tell whether they see you, let them go. Waiting a few moments costs little. A crash at an intersection can cost a great deal, because intersection crashes cause more serious injuries than crashes anywhere else.

lines.text: Look twice for small road users.
Speed and distance are hard to judge.

narration.text: Look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds at intersections, because their speed and distance are hard to judge. A quick glance is tuned to cars, and it can miss a smaller shape. When trees, buildings or snow piles block your view at an intersection, creep forward slowly until you can see past them. Stop first where you are supposed to stop, then move forward a little at a time until you have a clear view in every direction. Only then decide whether it is safe to go. Moving slowly gives any approaching driver or rider time to see you too.

lines.text: Trap: the other driver will yield.
When unsure, let them go first.

narration.text: Here is the trap. At an intersection, many drivers assume the other driver will do what the rules say, or what they expect. That is wrong. Let others go first whenever you are unsure what they will do. Options may suggest speeding up to go first, or proceeding because you have the right of way. Both are wrong. Having the right of way does not protect you if the other driver does not yield. Look twice, especially for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds, whose speed and distance are hard to judge, and wait whenever another driver's intentions are unclear.

Here is a quick check: at an intersection, you glance both ways and see no cars, but a motorcycle could be hidden from a quick look. What should you do? Recall the rule for small road users. Look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds at intersections, because their speed and distance are hard to judge. So the answer is to look again, carefully, before you go. A second look takes a moment, and it is aimed at exactly the road users a first glance tends to miss. Intersections are the deadliest part of the road, so that extra look is well worth it.

To finish, intersection crashes cause more traffic deaths and serious injuries than crashes on any other part of the road. Approaching an intersection, check oncoming and cross traffic, pedestrians, signals, signs, markings, road condition and blind areas, and let others go first whenever you are unsure what they will do. Look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds, because their speed and distance are hard to judge. When trees, buildings or snow piles block your view, creep forward slowly until you can see past them. The hook is look twice for riders, and the habit is to let others go first whenever you are unsure.

why_how.text: Freeways carry fast, one-direction traffic with no stops, so slow users are banned and merging takes care.
Ramps can sit side by side, so signs keep you from entering the wrong way.
Michigan law puts the duty to yield and adjust on the merging driver.
Merge signs warn freeway drivers of entering traffic, so they adjust speed or change lanes safely to help.

scenario.text: Lena enters the acceleration lane while a truck approaches in the right freeway lane.

reasoning.text: Reach freeway speed, signal, check mirrors and over your shoulder, then merge into a safe gap, yielding to freeway traffic.

result.text: Lena adjusts her speed to slip in behind the truck instead of forcing her way in front.

claim.text: Common mistake: expecting freeway traffic to make room for you when you merge.

correction.text: The merging driver, not freeway traffic, must adjust speed and placement to merge safely.

prompt.text: You are on a freeway, and a merge sign warns of traffic entering ahead. What can you do to help?

answer.text: Adjust your speed or change lanes safely to help them merge.

rationale.text: Merge signs warn of entering traffic; adjust speed or change lanes safely to help them, and watch for sudden moves toward exits.

narration.text: This lesson covers entering a freeway. Freeways carry one-direction traffic with no stops or intersections, which is why they move so fast and why getting on takes care. We will look at who is banned from freeways, why ramps need careful sign reading, how to use the acceleration lane, how to help others merge, and what Michigan's merge law requires. Practice questions often ask who must yield when merging, so we will make that rule clear. The short answer is that the merging driver adjusts, and that idea runs through the whole lesson from the first ramp to the final gap.

Freeways carry one-direction traffic with no stops or intersections. Pedestrians, motorcycles of one hundred twenty-four cc or less, mopeds, bicycles, ATVs and slow-moving vehicles are banned from them. So everything on a freeway is meant to move at freeway speed. Entrance ramps often sit beside exit ramps, so watch for Do Not Enter, Wrong Way and speed limit signs. Taking an exit ramp by mistake would put you head on with traffic leaving the freeway. Read the signs at the start of every ramp, and make sure you are on the entrance before you speed up.

Use the acceleration lane to reach freeway speed. Signal, check your mirrors, and glance over your shoulder. Then merge into a safe gap, yielding to freeway traffic and not counting on others to let you in. Reaching freeway speed matters because merging slowly forces traffic behind and beside you to brake. The shoulder glance matters because a car can sit in your blind spot right where you want to go. Pick your gap early, match its speed, and move in smoothly. If no gap appears, adjust your speed to find one, rather than forcing your way into the lane.

title.text: The merge law and merge signs

narration.text: Michigan's merge law means the merging driver must yield to traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard, and adjust speed and position to merge safely. This applies whether you are entering or leaving the freeway. On the freeway side, merge signs near entrances warn of entering traffic. Adjust your speed or change lanes safely to help them merge, and watch for drivers who brake or swerve suddenly toward an exit. So the law puts the duty on the merging driver, but courteous freeway drivers make room when they safely can. Both habits together keep the merge area calm.

lines.text: Trap: freeway traffic must let you in.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think freeway traffic must make room for them at an entrance ramp. That is wrong. The merging driver, not freeway traffic, must adjust speed and placement to merge safely. Under Michigan's merge law, the merging driver yields to traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard. Options may say the faster driver goes first, or that trucks must always move over. Both are wrong. Freeway drivers may help when they safely can, but the duty belongs to the driver who is merging. That is true when entering the freeway and also when leaving it.

Here is a quick check: you are driving on the freeway, and a merge sign warns of traffic entering ahead. What can you do to help? Recall the merge sign rule. Merge signs near entrances warn of entering traffic. Adjust your speed or change lanes safely to help them merge, and watch for drivers who brake or swerve suddenly toward an exit. So the answer is to adjust your speed or, if it is safe, move over a lane. The merging driver still has the duty to yield, but giving them room makes the merge smoother and safer for everyone around you.

To finish, freeways carry one-direction traffic with no stops or intersections, and pedestrians, small motorcycles, mopeds, bicycles, ATVs and slow-moving vehicles are banned. Entrance ramps often sit beside exit ramps, so watch for Do Not Enter, Wrong Way and speed limit signs. Use the acceleration lane to reach freeway speed, signal, check mirrors and glance over your shoulder, then merge into a safe gap without counting on others to let you in. Under Michigan's merge law, the merging driver yields and adjusts, entering or leaving, while freeway drivers help where they safely can. The hook is the merger adjusts.

why_how.text: Keeping right on two-lane freeways leaves the left lane for passing and special cases.
On wider freeways any lane is allowed, but slow drivers stay with slower traffic.
Exiting and stopping safely means slowing only in the right place and never reversing.

scenario.text: Max realizes he has just passed his exit on the freeway.

reasoning.text: Never back up, turn around or use the median crossover, which is only for emergency and MDOT vehicles; go to the next exit and come back.

result.text: Max continues to the next exit, leaves the freeway, and returns the other way.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a single driver may never use an HOV lane.

correction.text: HOV lanes require two or more occupants only during peak hours; outside those hours they are open to everyone, and motorcycles may use them any time.

prompt.text: You plan to exit the freeway. When should you begin slowing down?

answer.text: Only once you are fully in the deceleration lane.

rationale.text: Signal into the deceleration lane, do not slow until fully in it, then obey the ramp speed limit.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving on the freeway once you are on it: which lane to use, how HOV lanes work, when you may stop, how to exit, and what to do if you miss your exit. The lane rules differ depending on how many lanes the freeway has in your direction, so we will compare two-lane freeways with wider ones. Practice questions often test the HOV hours and the missed-exit rule, so we will be clear about both. Freeway speeds leave little room for surprises, which is why each rule here is about predictable, steady driving and moving only when you are sure.

lines.text: Two lanes: keep right with exceptions.
Near minimum speed: keep with slower traffic.

narration.text: On a two-lane freeway, keep right except to pass, to exit left, to let a vehicle merge, in heavy congestion, or when emergency vehicles or construction workers are on the shoulders. With three or more lanes in your direction, you may use any lane, but stay with the slower traffic if you are driving at or near the minimum speed. So the rule loosens as the freeway gets wider. On two lanes, the right lane is home. On three or more, you may choose, as long as you do not hold up faster traffic while driving slowly. In both cases, the left side is where faster traffic expects to be.

lines.text: Two or more occupants at peak hours.
Open to all at other times.

narration.text: HOV lanes require two or more occupants during peak hours, such as rush hour. Outside those hours, they are open to everyone. Motorcycles may use them any time. So an HOV lane is not always restricted. The restriction applies only during peak hours, and motorcycles are exempt at all times. So check whether it is peak hours before you move into the lane. A driver alone in a car may use the lane outside those hours. During those hours, that driver must stay in the regular lanes, even if the HOV lane looks empty and inviting.

lines.text: Flashers on, fully off the pavement.
Slow only in the deceleration lane.

narration.text: Stop on a freeway only in an emergency. Then use your hazard flashers, slow gradually, and pull completely off the pavement. A car stopped in a travel lane at freeway speed is a severe danger. To exit, check traffic and signal into the deceleration lane, and do not slow down until you are fully in that lane. Then obey the ramp speed limit, since many ramps curve sharply. Slowing in the travel lane before the exit forces the traffic behind you to brake suddenly. The deceleration lane exists so that you can slow down out of the way of everyone else.

lines.text: Never back up or turn around.

narration.text: If you miss your exit, never back up, turn around, or use the median crossover. The median crossover is only for emergency and MDOT vehicles. Instead, go to the next exit and come back. Missing an exit is annoying, but it is never an emergency. Backing up on a freeway shoulder or in a lane puts you against the flow of fast traffic that does not expect a stopped or reversing car. Turning across the median is even worse. The next exit may add a few minutes to your trip, and it is the only safe and legal way to recover.

lines.text: Trap: HOV lanes are always restricted.

narration.text: Here is the trap. HOV restrictions apply only during peak hours, and motorcycles are exempt at all times. Options may say a single driver can never use an HOV lane, or that motorcycles must follow the occupancy rule. Both are wrong. A second trap involves lane choice. On a two-lane freeway you keep right except in listed cases, but with three or more lanes any lane is allowed unless you are near the minimum speed. An option claiming you must always keep right on every freeway, or that any lane is fine on a two-lane freeway, misses this difference.

Here is a quick check: your exit is coming up on the freeway. When should you begin slowing down? Recall the exit steps. To exit, check traffic and signal into the deceleration lane, and do not slow down until you are fully in that lane. Then obey the ramp speed limit, since many ramps curve sharply. So the answer is only once you are fully in the deceleration lane. Slowing earlier, while still in the travel lane, can surprise drivers behind you and cause a rear-end crash. Hold your speed, move over, and then slow down for the ramp.

To finish, on a two-lane freeway keep right except to pass, exit left, let a vehicle merge, in heavy congestion, or when emergency vehicles or workers are on the shoulders. With three or more lanes, any lane is allowed, but slow drivers stay with slower traffic. HOV lanes need two or more occupants during peak hours, are open to all at other times, and motorcycles may use them any time. Stop only in an emergency, with flashers on and fully off the pavement. Slow only once you are in the deceleration lane, and if you miss your exit, go to the next one. The hook is missed exit, take the next.

why_how.text: The steady sound of freeway driving can make you sleepy, so fatigue is one of the biggest freeway dangers.
Breaks and switching drivers work; coffee and stay-awake drugs do not.
Cruise control helps on open roads but distracts in traffic and on slick roads, and the brake cancels it.

scenario.text: Two hours into a long drive, Ann starts to yawn and lose focus.

reasoning.text: Do not rely on coffee or stay-awake drugs; take a ten-minute break at least every two hours or let someone else drive.

result.text: Ann stops at a rest area for a break and lets her passenger take the next turn at the wheel.

claim.text: Myth: coffee is a reliable fix for drowsy driving.

correction.text: Do not rely on coffee or stay-awake drugs; take a break at least every two hours or let someone else drive.

prompt.text: You are using cruise control and tap the accelerator to pass. Is cruise control still on?

answer.text: Yes. Only the brake turns it off.

rationale.text: Pressing the accelerator does not cancel cruise control, but pressing the brake pedal does.

narration.text: This lesson covers two things that matter most on long freeway drives: fatigue and cruise control. Fatigue is one of the biggest freeway dangers, and the fixes many drivers rely on do not work. Cruise control can make long drives easier, but only in the right conditions, and you need to know what turns it off. We will look at why freeways make drivers sleepy, what to do about it, how to stay alert if you must keep going, and when cruise control helps or hurts. Practice questions often ask what cancels cruise control, so we will make that point especially clear.

lines.text: The steady hum makes you sleepy.
Take a ten-minute break every two hours.

narration.text: Fatigue is one of the biggest freeway dangers, since the steady hum of wind, tires and engine can make you sleepy or even hypnotized. Do not rely on coffee or stay-awake drugs. If you are tired, take a ten-minute break at least every two hours, or let someone else drive. Breaks work because they change what your body is doing. A short stop interrupts the steady freeway sound that causes drowsiness. Coffee may make you feel more alert for a short time, but it does not remove the fatigue that is slowing your reactions.

If you must keep driving while tired, keep moving your eyes across the road. Check your mirrors, and look near, far, left and right. Moving your eyes keeps your brain engaged with the road instead of sliding into the trance that the steady hum can cause. Staring at one spot, such as the car ahead or the center line, makes drowsiness worse. This is not a replacement for rest. It is a way to stay as alert as possible until you can reach a safe place to stop. As soon as you can, take a break or hand the driving over to someone else.

lines.text: Set at or below the limit.
Avoid in traffic, ramps, slick roads, towing.

narration.text: Cruise control works best in rural areas with light traffic. Set it at or below the speed limit. Avoid cruise control in heavy traffic, near many ramps, on roads slick with rain, snow or ice, and when towing heavy loads, since constant resetting distracts you. Those are the conditions where you need full, active control of your speed. Pressing the accelerator does not cancel cruise control, but pressing the brake pedal does. So you can speed up briefly to pass and the system stays set, but any touch of the brake turns it off.

Here is the trap. Tapping the accelerator leaves cruise control on, but touching the brake turns it off. Options may say pressing the accelerator cancels cruise control, or that you must press a button to turn it off before braking. Both are wrong. The brake pedal always cancels it. This matters in an emergency, because your natural reaction to brake will also turn cruise control off. It also matters when passing. If you press the accelerator to pass, the car returns to its set speed when you let up, because cruise control never turned off in the first place.

Here is a quick check: you are using cruise control, and you tap the accelerator to pass a slower car. Is cruise control still on? Recall which pedal cancels it. Pressing the accelerator does not cancel cruise control, but pressing the brake pedal does. So the answer is yes, it is still on. When you let up on the accelerator after passing, the car will settle back to the speed you set. If you had touched the brake instead, cruise control would have turned off, and you would need to set it again once it was safe and the conditions allowed it.

To finish, fatigue is one of the biggest freeway dangers, since the steady hum of wind, tires and engine can make you sleepy. Do not rely on coffee or stay-awake drugs. Take a ten-minute break at least every two hours, or let someone else drive, and if you must keep going, keep your eyes moving and check your mirrors. Cruise control works best in light rural traffic, set at or below the limit, and should be avoided in heavy traffic, near many ramps, on slick roads and when towing. The accelerator does not cancel it, but the brake does. The hook is simple: breaks, not coffee.

why_how.text: In an emergency, the right move is often the opposite of instinct, such as not swerving left.
Most skids come from going too fast or stopping suddenly on slippery roads, and recovery means steering where you want to go.
Anti-lock and standard brakes need different techniques in a hard stop.

scenario.text: On a wet curve, Ty's car begins to slide toward the shoulder.

reasoning.text: In a skid, lift off the accelerator, point the front wheels only where you want to go, expect a secondary skid, steer again, then straighten.

result.text: Ty eases off the gas, steers toward his lane, corrects the second slide, and straightens out.

claim.text: Common mistake: pumping anti-lock brakes when they pulse during a hard stop.

correction.text: Anti-lock brakes need hard, firm pressure held until you stop, and vibration or pulsing is normal.

prompt.text: You are about to hit a stopped car and cannot stop in time. What should you do?

answer.text: Steer around it, turning no more than you need.

rationale.text: If you cannot stop before hitting another vehicle, steer around it, turning no more than you need.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving emergencies: an oncoming vehicle in your lane, a crash you cannot stop for, a skid, and a hard stop. In each case, the right action may feel unnatural, which is why it helps to learn it ahead of time. We will look at where to go when a vehicle comes at you, how to steer around an obstacle, what causes skids and how to recover, and how braking differs with anti-lock brakes and without them. Practice questions often test the anti-lock braking technique, so we will compare the two systems directly and explain why each works.

lines.text: Tap the horn if there is time.

narration.text: If an oncoming vehicle is in your lane, tap the horn if there is time. Brake hard without locking the wheels if you lack anti-lock brakes. Look for an escape route on the right edge. Avoid swerving left, because the other driver may notice you and return to the proper lane, which would put the two of you head on in that lane. Stop in your lane only if there is room and you cannot pull off. If you cannot stop before hitting another vehicle, steer around it, turning no more than you need. A small, controlled turn keeps the car under control.

lines.text: Too fast or too sudden on slick roads.
Steer where you want to go.

narration.text: Most skids come from turning too fast or stopping suddenly on slippery pavement. Test the brakes lightly to feel the road when conditions are slick. In a skid, lift off the accelerator. Point the front wheels only where you want to go. Expect a secondary skid the other way, steer again, and then straighten the wheels. The key is to look and steer toward your path, not toward what you are afraid of hitting. Small, smooth steering corrections work better than large ones. A skid can feel frightening, but a calm, practiced response gives you the best chance to regain control.

Under normal conditions, a steady, firm push on the brake pedal is how you slow and stop. In a hard stop, technique depends on your brakes. Anti-lock brakes need hard, firm pressure from the start, held until you stop, and vibration or pulsing is normal. With full anti-lock brakes, you keep pressing and steer. Without anti-lock brakes, you brake just short of locking, and release and reapply if the wheels lock, which is called threshold or controlled braking. With standard brakes, steady pressure without locking the wheels keeps them turning so you can steer.

lines.text: Trap: swerve left from an oncoming car.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a vehicle comes at you in your lane, instinct may say swerve left into the empty lane. Avoid swerving left from an oncoming vehicle, because its driver may notice you and return to the proper lane. Look for an escape route on the right edge instead. A second trap is braking. When anti-lock brakes pulse and vibrate, some drivers lift off or pump the pedal. That is wrong. Anti-lock brakes need hard, firm pressure from the start held until you stop, and the pulsing is normal. Pumping belongs only to standard brakes, when the wheels lock.

lines.text: Release and reapply if they lock.

narration.text: Skids and braking connect through one idea: wheels that keep turning can steer. With standard brakes, steady pressure without locking the wheels keeps them turning so you can steer. If the wheels do lock, release and reapply, which is threshold or controlled braking. With full anti-lock brakes, the system does that work for you, so you keep pressing and steer. In a skid, you lift off the accelerator and point the front wheels where you want to go. In every case, the goal is the same: keep the tires rolling enough that your steering still works.

Here is a quick check: you are about to hit a stopped car ahead, and you cannot stop in time. What should you do? Recall the emergency steering rule. If you cannot stop before hitting another vehicle, steer around it, turning no more than you need. So the answer is to steer around the car with the smallest turn that works. Jerking the wheel hard can cause a skid or send you into other traffic. A smooth, limited move around the obstacle is the safest choice when stopping is no longer possible. Keep looking at the path you want to take as you steer.

lines.text: Steer where you want to go.

narration.text: To finish, if an oncoming vehicle is in your lane, tap the horn, brake hard without locking if you lack anti-lock brakes, and look for an escape route on the right edge. Avoid swerving left, since the other driver may return to the proper lane. If you cannot stop, steer around, turning no more than you need. Most skids come from turning too fast or stopping suddenly, and in a skid you lift off the gas and steer where you want to go. Normal stops use a steady, firm push. Anti-lock brakes need hard, held pressure, while standard brakes need threshold braking. The hook is never swerve left.

why_how.text: Weather reduces traction and visibility, so you slow down, leave more room and prepare your car.
Rain is most dangerous at the start, and water can make tires lose contact or brakes stop working well.
Floods, fog, ice and snow each bring hazards you may not see until too late.

scenario.text: A light rain starts as Mia drives home, after weeks of dry weather.

reasoning.text: Roads are slickest in the first half hour of rain because oil has not yet washed off, so slow down and allow at least twice the normal following distance.

result.text: Mia slows down, doubles her following distance, and takes extra care at intersections.

claim.text: Myth: if the water on a flooded road looks shallow, it is safe to drive around the barricades.

correction.text: Never drive around barricades closing a flooded road, since debris, power lines or a washed-out road may be hidden.

prompt.text: Fog grows so thick you cannot see the road ahead at all. What should you do?

answer.text: Pull off, turn on the four-way flashers and wait.

rationale.text: Drive slowly in fog with low beams, and if you cannot see at all, pull off, turn on the four-way flashers and wait.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving in bad weather. Weather affects both how well your tires grip the road and how well you can see. We will look at preparing your car before winter, general rules for fog, rain and snow, the danger of the first half hour of rain, hydroplaning, wet brakes, flooded roads, fog, and ice and snow. Michigan drivers face all of these, often in the same season. Practice questions here often test the first half hour of rain and what to do in thick fog, so we will make both rules clear and connect each one to the reason behind it.

lines.text: Extra time, slower speed, longer gaps.

narration.text: Pre-winter maintenance is the best way to travel safely. Check power steering, brake, washer and oil fluids, keep antifreeze strong and fresh, and consider washer fluid with antifreeze. In fog, rain or snow, leave extra time, drive slower and increase your following distance. Remember that bridges and underpasses freeze before the road in cold weather. So bad weather driving starts before you leave the driveway, with a car that is ready for it, and continues with a slower, more patient style once you are on the road. A longer gap gives you time to stop on a slick surface.

Roads are slickest in the first half hour of rain, because oil from vehicles has not yet washed off. Slow down, take extra care at intersections, and allow at least twice the normal following distance. Hydroplaning happens when tires ride on top of water and can cost you control. Worn tires, low tire pressure and too much speed make it more likely. After deep water or heavy rain, test your brakes, which may pull or fail to hold. Press gently while driving slowly until they work normally. Water affects your car in several ways, so slow down whenever the road is wet.

lines.text: Deep water can damage the engine.

narration.text: Never drive around barricades closing a flooded road. Debris, power lines or a washed-out road may be hidden under the water. Without barricades, consider another route, and remember that deep water can damage the engine. A flooded road can look calm and shallow while the pavement beneath it is gone. What you cannot see is the danger. So the safest choice with any flooded road is to avoid it. Turn around and find another way, even if it takes longer. If you do drive through water, test your brakes gently afterward, because they may pull or fail to hold.

lines.text: Fog: slow, low beams, ready to stop.
Cannot see? Pull off with flashers.
Ice and snow: slow and gradual.

narration.text: Drive slowly in fog with low-beam headlights, ready to stop. If you cannot see at all, pull off, turn on the four-way flashers and wait. Being ready to stop matters because a hazard can appear out of the fog with little warning. On ice and snow, drive slowly, slow down gradually, and listen and watch for snowmobiles and trail crossing signs, since stopping power is reduced. Every move on ice should be gentle: gentle braking, gentle steering and gentle acceleration. Sudden moves are what turn a slippery road into a skid.

title.text: The first rain and the flood

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think a light rain is less dangerous than a heavy one. But roads are slickest in the first half hour of rain, because oil from vehicles has not yet washed off, so you should slow down and allow at least twice the normal following distance. Options may say the road is safest when rain first starts, or that normal following distance is fine. Both are wrong. A second trap involves floods. Never drive around barricades closing a flooded road, even if the water looks shallow, since debris, power lines or a washed-out road may be hidden.

Here is a quick check: fog grows so thick that you cannot see the road ahead at all. What should you do? Recall the fog rule. Drive slowly in fog with low-beam headlights, ready to stop, and if you cannot see at all, pull off, turn on the four-way flashers and wait. So the answer is to pull off the road, turn on your four-way flashers, and wait for the fog to lift. Stopping in your lane would leave you exposed to drivers behind you who cannot see either. Pulling fully off and using your flashers makes you visible and out of the way.

lines.text: Low beams in fog; never pass barricades.

narration.text: To finish, pre-winter maintenance is the best way to travel safely. In fog, rain or snow, leave extra time, drive slower and increase following distance, and remember bridges and underpasses freeze first. Roads are slickest in the first half hour of rain, so allow at least twice the normal following distance. Hydroplaning is more likely with worn tires, low pressure and too much speed, and after deep water you test your brakes gently. Never drive around flood barricades. In fog, use low beams and pull off with flashers if you cannot see, and on ice and snow drive slowly and gently. The hook is first half hour, double gap.
